specPoints.text: explain the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves
know that waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter

primer.text: You already know that a disturbance can ripple outwards from a source: ripples crossing a pond, a pulse shaken along a rope, sound reaching your ears. Each of those is a wave carrying energy away from whatever made it. This lesson sorts waves into two families by the direction their vibrations swing relative to that travel.

lessons.title: Transverse waves
lessons.opening: Some waves shake sideways across their own path. When you flick a rope, each bit of rope moves up and down while the pulse runs away from your hand at right angles to that motion. Any wave whose vibrations sit at right angles to its direction of travel is called transverse, and ropes, water surfaces and light all behave this way.
keyPoints: A transverse wave vibrates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer, at right angles to it.
The highest point above the resting level is the peak, also called the crest.
The lowest point below the resting level is the trough.
Ripples on water, a plucked guitar string and S-waves are transverse examples.
Electromagnetic waves are transverse and can even travel through a vacuum.

low.restatement: In a transverse wave the wiggling happens across the line the wave moves along, like shaking a rope up and down while the pulse travels forward.
low.analogy: A stadium crowd doing a Mexican wave: each person stands and sits in place while the wave sweeps around the ground.
low.examPointer: If a question shows peaks and troughs, name the wave transverse and say the vibration is perpendicular to travel.

medium.restatement: Transverse waves carry energy outward without carrying the material with them: the rope returns to rest after the pulse has gone.
medium.analogy: A line of dominos toppling passes energy along, yet every domino stays on its own spot on the table.
medium.examPointer: Marks are available for pairing "perpendicular vibration" with "energy transferred, not the medium", so quote both.

check.stem: In a transverse wave, the vibrations are oriented:

options.explanation: That describes a longitudinal wave instead.

options.text: at right angles to the direction of travel
options.explanation: Transverse vibrations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
The vibration follows one line, fixed by the wave type.

options.text: opposite to the direction of travel
options.explanation: Vibration is not backwards along the path; it is across it.

check.stem: The highest point of a transverse wave is called:

options.explanation: The trough is the lowest point, not the highest.
Compressions belong to longitudinal waves.
Peak and crest both name the point above the resting level.
A wavefront is a line drawn to represent one wave from above.

check.stem: Which of these is a transverse wave?

options.explanation: Sound is longitudinal: air particles oscillate along the travel direction.
P-waves are the longitudinal seismic type.

options.text: a pulse squeezed along a spring
options.explanation: Push-pull pulses along a spring are longitudinal.

options.text: a ripple moving over a pond
options.explanation: Water-surface ripples are a standard transverse example.

check.stem: A transverse wave passes along a rope. What happens to the rope itself?

options.text: each piece oscillates and returns to its rest position
options.explanation: The rope vibrates about a fixed point while energy passes through.

options.text: it travels with the wave to the far end
options.explanation: The medium oscillates about fixed points; only the energy travels onward.
No permanent stretch is involved in passing a wave.
The rope is the thing that vibrates.

check.stem: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that can travel:

options.explanation: Mechanical transverse waves face that restriction; EM waves do not.
That mix blocks some mechanical waves, and EM are not limited to it.

options.text: through a vacuum as well as through matter
options.explanation: Light and radio cross empty space, unlike longitudinal waves.
EM waves need no medium at all.

check.stem: State what a peak and a trough are on a transverse wave.
check.modelAnswer: The peak (crest) is the highest point above the undisturbed rest position; the trough is the lowest point below it.

check.stem: List three transverse wave examples.
check.modelAnswer: Any three of: water ripples, vibrations in a guitar string, S-waves, electromagnetic waves such as light or radio.

check.stem: Explain why shaking a rope up and down produces a transverse pulse.
check.modelAnswer: Your hand drives the rope vertically while the pulse runs horizontally along it, so the vibration sits at right angles to the travel direction, which is exactly the transverse geometry.

check.stem: A radio wave crosses empty space between a satellite and the ground. Use wave-family knowledge to explain how this is possible.
check.modelAnswer: Radio waves are transverse electromagnetic waves, and electromagnetic waves need no material medium, so they travel through the vacuum of space where a longitudinal wave could not.

lessons.title: Longitudinal waves
lessons.opening: The second family vibrates along the journey instead of across it. Push and pull one end of a spring and the coils bunch together, then spread apart, and that pattern races down the spring. Waves built from these push-pull regions are longitudinal, and sound in air is the everyday example.
keyPoints: A longitudinal wave vibrates parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
Regions where particles crowd together are called compressions.
Regions where particles are spread out are called rarefactions.
Sound waves and P-waves are longitudinal examples.
A longitudinal wave needs particles, so it cannot travel through a vacuum.

low.restatement: In a longitudinal wave the material shuffles back and forth along the same line that the wave travels, forming stretched and squeezed zones.
low.analogy: Push one end of a slinky and watch a squeezed zone hurry along its length while each coil only slides a little.
low.examPointer: Label compressions and rarefactions on any longitudinal diagram; the labels themselves usually carry the mark.

medium.restatement: The particles of the medium vibrate about their own positions while the compression-rarefaction pattern advances, so energy moves without any particle making the whole journey.
medium.analogy: A traffic jam wave on a motorway: the queue pattern sweeps backwards past cars that each only creep briefly.
medium.examPointer: When asked why sound cannot cross a vacuum, answer that longitudinal waves need particles to compress in the first place.

check.stem: In a longitudinal wave the vibrations are oriented:

options.text: at right angles to the direction of travel
options.explanation: Right-angle vibration defines the transverse family.

options.text: parallel to the direction of travel
options.explanation: Longitudinal vibrations run along the direction of energy transfer.
Vibration is along a line, not a spiral.

options.text: at 45 degrees to the direction of travel
options.explanation: The geometry is strictly along the path.

check.stem: A region of a longitudinal wave where particles are bunched closest together is called:

options.explanation: A rarefaction is the spread-out region, the opposite of bunched.
Crests belong to transverse waves.
A wavefront is a drawing convention, not a particle region.
Compressions are where the medium is squeezed closest.

check.stem: Which wave cannot travel through a vacuum?

options.explanation: Sound is longitudinal and needs particles to compress, so a vacuum blocks it.
Light is electromagnetic and crosses empty space freely.
Radio is electromagnetic, so a vacuum is no barrier.
Electromagnetic waves manage perfectly well in a vacuum.

check.stem: Sound travels from a drum to your ear through air. What does the air do?

options.text: air particles travel from the drum all the way to your ear
options.explanation: Particles oscillate locally; nothing more than energy crosses the room.

options.text: air particles spin on the spot
options.explanation: The motion is a linear back-and-forth shuffle.

options.text: air particles vibrate back and forth about their own positions
options.explanation: The push-pull oscillation passes energy along without transporting particles.
The air is the medium doing the vibrating.

check.stem: Where the particles of a longitudinal wave are most spread apart, the region is:

options.explanation: Compressions are the crowded zones.
Rarefactions are the stretched-out zones between compressions.
Troughs are transverse features.
Rest position describes an undisturbed level, not a wave region of this kind.

check.stem: State the two alternating regions that make up a longitudinal wave.
check.modelAnswer: Compressions, where particles are pushed close together, alternating with rarefactions, where particles are spread further apart.

check.stem: Give three examples of longitudinal waves.
check.modelAnswer: Any three of: sound waves, P-waves, and pressure waves set up by repeated pushes in a liquid or gas.

check.stem: Explain why a longitudinal wave cannot carry energy through empty space.
check.modelAnswer: The wave works by squeezing and stretching the material it passes through, so with no particles present in a vacuum there is nothing to compress and the pattern cannot propagate.

check.stem: A spring lies on a bench and you repeatedly push and pull one end along its length. Describe what a viewer at the far end observes.
check.modelAnswer: They observe compressions and rarefactions travelling towards them along the spring; each coil merely shuffles along the spring axis, showing energy transfer without the coils themselves being carried to them.

lessons.title: Comparing the two families & energy transfer
sourceHeadings: A comparison of longitudinal and transverse waves
Properties of transverse and longitudinal waves
lessons.opening: Put the two families side by side and the contrast is sharpest in structure: peaks and troughs against compressions and rarefactions. What unites them matters more for exams: every wave, of either family, moves energy and information from source to receiver while the material it travels through stays put.
keyPoints: Transverse waves show peaks and troughs; longitudinal waves show compressions and rarefactions.
Transverse vibrations are perpendicular to travel; longitudinal vibrations are parallel to it.
Only transverse electromagnetic waves cross a vacuum; longitudinal waves need a medium.
Waves transfer energy and information without transferring matter.
A floating duck bobs up and down as water waves pass, showing energy moves but the duck does not travel.

low.restatement: The two wave families differ in vibration direction and structure, yet both carry energy and information outward from a source without hauling the medium along.
low.analogy: Two courier services, one on bicycles across a field and one through a tunnel: different routes, same parcel delivered.
low.examPointer: Comparison tables earn marks quickly: give structure, vibration direction and vacuum behaviour for both families.

medium.restatement: Because the medium only oscillates locally, what advances is the disturbance: the energy of the source and any signal it encodes reach the receiver while each particle ends where it began.
medium.analogy: A message travelling along a line of people holding hands: each person sways in turn, and the squeeze passes down the line without anyone changing place.
medium.examPointer: The duck-in-water observation is the classic evidence question: the duck bobs but does not drift, so energy transferred and matter did not.

check.stem: Which row correctly pairs a transverse wave with its structure?

options.explanation: That structure belongs to longitudinal waves.
Longitudinal waves have no peaks; they have density zones.
The structures are the clearest contrast between the families.
Peaks and troughs are the anatomy of transverse waves.

check.stem: What does any wave transfer from source to receiver?

options.text: energy and information, but not matter
options.explanation: That is the transfer law for all waves.
The medium stays put; nothing material makes the trip.
If only matter moved, nothing would oscillate in place.
Carrying energy is the defining job of a wave.

check.stem: A toy duck floats in a bath as ripples pass underneath. The duck:

options.text: drifts along with each ripple across the bath
options.explanation: The duck oscillates in place; it does not surf the wave.
Nothing in the wave pushes the duck under.

options.text: bobs up and down while staying in place
options.explanation: Local oscillation with no net travel is the evidence that energy, not matter, moves.

options.text: is lifted out of the water
options.explanation: The passing wave only bobs it about its floating level.

check.stem: Sound and light both reach you from a fireworks display: light as a transverse wave, sound as a longitudinal one. Which claim is correct for both?

options.explanation: Light is transverse; only sound is longitudinal here.

options.text: both transfer energy without transferring matter
options.explanation: All waves obey this transfer law whatever their family.
Light crosses vacuum; sound does not.
Waves carry information as well as energy.

check.stem: Waves on a water surface are transverse. A floating ball moves:

options.text: mainly horizontally, racing ahead of the ripples
options.explanation: Nothing in the wave carries the ball forward.
The oscillation stays small and local.
The ball visibly bobs; that is the point of the demonstration.

options.text: mainly up and down as the ripples pass
options.explanation: The ball oscillates about its place, mirroring the perpendicular vibration of the surface.

check.stem: State two differences between transverse and longitudinal waves.
check.modelAnswer: Transverse vibrations are perpendicular to travel with peaks and troughs; longitudinal vibrations are parallel to travel with compressions and rarefactions.

check.stem: State what is meant by the statement that waves transfer energy without transferring matter.
check.modelAnswer: The oscillation passes energy and any encoded information from source to receiver while each particle of the medium only vibrates about its own fixed position.

check.stem: Explain how the floating-duck observation supports the wave transfer law: energy and information move, matter does not.
check.modelAnswer: The duck gains energy, shown by its bobbing, yet it does not travel across the surface with the wave, so what crossed the water was energy and information and not the material of the medium.

check.stem: An earthquake produces both P-waves and S-waves at the same time. Using wave families, predict which type arrives first at a distant station given that longitudinal waves run fastest in solids.
check.modelAnswer: The P-waves arrive first, because they are the longitudinal type and longitudinal waves travel fastest through solid rock, while the transverse S-waves run slower and arrive later.

glossary.definition: A wave whose vibrations sit at right angles to the direction it carries energy.
A wave whose vibrations run along the same line as the direction it carries energy.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are bunched closest together.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are spread furthest apart.
Completely empty space with no particles of matter in it at all.

workedExample.prompt: A loudspeaker generates sound waves that travel to the right. A dust mote floats in the air beside the loudspeaker, labelled D. Draw arrows to indicate how the dust mote would vibrate as the sound waves pass it.
steps: Recall the family: sound waves are longitudinal, so points along the wave vibrate along the same line as the wave travels.
The sound travels to the right, so the dust mote must oscillate back and forth along that same right-left line.
Draw the arrows at D parallel to the direction the sound waves travel (one arrow pointing right, one pointing left along the same line).
workedExample.finalAnswer: Arrows at D drawn parallel to the direction of travel of the sound waves, because longitudinal vibrations are along the direction of energy transfer.
